I'm going to go ahead and call bullshit on that source. IQ is a normalized measure, that is, it is scored such that there is a standard normal (bell curve) distribution in scores. If I recall correctly, most tests use a standard deviation of around 15, but by the very definition of IQ, 100 is average--especially because scores are inflated or deflated when making the tests to ensure their distribution.

So, why is it that only 10 of the 80 countries surveyed were above average, and at least a third (I didn't count this one precisely) are more than a standard deviation below the mean? Going solely on average country scores, that distribution is not (standard, normal) AND (mean = 100).

Now, you might argue that outliers may be the issue, i.e., poorer-scoring countries have some large groups who scored, let's say, a 10, while the rest of the population was largely average, while other countries had a more reasonable distribution. To this, I'd point out that such a situation would give either a skewed distribution (which we see here) or a bimodal distribution, neither of which are standard normal curves, and both of which still maintain a worldwide mean IQ of less than 100.
